# Small-data / 30‑minute single‑accelerator recommendations to reduce held-out NLL (BPB)

Summary statement (research-evidence first): the literature and recent tooling papers provide actionable, low-risk interventions for this strict short-run regime: optimize data sampling/shuffling to avoid I/O/reshuffle slowdowns and to reduce harmful repetition; prefer tuned (not necessarily smaller) global batches and test microbatching for throughput gains; exercise caution about relying on gradient-noise benefits from tiny batches in single-epoch/short-token regimes; use curriculum/reservoir sampling as a targeted experiment in genuinely small runs; and prioritize experiments that trade wall‑clock time for cleaner data passes rather than mechanical higher token counts. These conclusions are drawn only from the provided primary sources and the user’s baseline notes; where evidence is absent, the report flags gaps and conjectures separately. [1–8]

## 1. Data repetition and data scheduling (shuffling, repeats, curriculum, reservoir sampling)
Evidence summary: cramming rules show training from scratch permits speedups via judicious sampling choices without pretrained models [1]; exponential reservoir sampling gives an O(1) single‑pass method for bounded memory streaming with recency bias and uniformity guarantees [2]; a recent analysis argues high‑quality data rapidly loses utility under repeated use and that using many distinct tokens with few epochs is preferable to many epochs on the same high‑quality data [3]; curriculum learning produced significant gains for very small code LMs trained under two hours on a single GPU in the referenced experiments [5]; Hugging Face curriculum work presents hybrid schedules as a practical starting point [8].  
Interpretation for the 30‑minute/≈300M‑token regime: empirical evidence supports prioritizing diversity of tokens (avoid excessive repeats of the same high‑quality subset) and trying single‑pass/streaming-reservoir or lightweight curriculum when data ordering or difficulty is relevant; curriculum showed measurable gain in very short code‑LM runs [5] while repeated use of the same high‑quality data can lose utility [3]. [1–3], [5], [8]  
Minimal discriminating experiment (smallest test to run): compare (A) baseline global random shuffle pass vs (B) reservoir sampling stream (fixed reservoir size) and (C) a simple curriculum (easy→hard hybrid from [8]) — each run limited to the same 30‑minute wall time and same token budget as the baseline logs. Stop / pass criteria: treat as success if validation BPB at end‑of‑run is consistently lower than baseline across repeated runs (see Confounders). Evidence vs conjecture: the source papers provide the algorithmic facts and short‑run curriculum result [2], [5]; extrapolating curriculum benefit beyond code LMs or to particular curriculum definitions is conjectural. [2], [5], [8], [3], [1]

Confounders and controls: I/O and global-shuffle overhead can masquerade as training differences — Rinas shows shuffled loading can reduce throughput 30–50% and that optimized loaders can deliver up to 89% speedups for LMs [4]; control experiments must log effective tokens/sec and ensure any BPB change is not due solely to different token counts. Also control for repetition artifacts highlighted in [3] by recording per‑token repeat counts and tracking validation BPB on a fixed held‑out set.

## 2. Critical batch size and microbatching tradeoffs
Evidence summary: microbatching (32 microbatches) showed a 4.8× throughput gain in one controlled study [6]; Rinas documents large throughput penalties from shuffling that can be mitigated by loader improvements, improving tokens/sec by up to 89% [4]; recent analysis finds that gradient noise advantages of small batches do not necessarily hold in single‑epoch training and that small batches can underperform for LM single‑epoch regimes (Filatov) while other work reports a U‑shaped relationship between batch size and loss for Adam [7].  
Interpretation: do not assume tiny microbatches automatically improve BPB in a single‑pass / short‑token regime; microbatching can be used to increase effective tokens processed within the 30‑minute wall time, but gains must be validated against the documented risk that small batches may underperform in single‑epoch settings. [6], [4], [7]  
Minimal discriminating experiment: holding total wall time constant, compare (A) baseline global batch size (as in baseline run logs) vs (B) microbatching configuration that yields higher tokens/sec (measure via Rinas-style logging) vs (C) a modestly larger global batch if hardware permits. Pass criterion: improved validation BPB not explained by higher token count alone (see Confounders). Evidence vs conjecture: the throughput facts are evidence [6], [4]; the single‑epoch batch‑size performance caution is evidence from [7]; whether a particular microbatch count helps this exact baseline is empirical.

Confounders: optimizer step frequency interacts with batch size and Adam hyperparameters (see next section); log per‑update step counts, tokens/sec, and validation BPB; avoid attributing gains to token count alone.

## 3. Learning‑rate schedule shapes and warmup interactions
Evidence summary: the provided sources do not contain detailed experimental results on warmup lengths or decay shapes for short single‑accelerator runs; the Vyas analysis highlights sensitivity of single‑epoch/single‑pass training to batch‑size and optimizer tuning [7].  
Interpretation and evidence gap: no primary evidence in the provided findings prescribes specific warmup lengths or decay shapes for this regime. This is an evidence gap. Suggested minimal experiment (parsimony): compare baseline schedule (as in user logs) vs a short warmup vs no warmup keeping other states identical; measure validation BPB at identical wall time. Stop: abort variant showing instability (training loss divergence) or higher validation BPB than baseline.

## 4. Optimizer choice and hyperparameters
Evidence summary: Vyas and referenced authors note that small batches’ behavior depends on Adam beta tuning; Filatov et al. reported small batches underperforming on C4 when Adam decay rates were not tuned [7]. No head‑to‑head LAMB/Adafactor data appears in the provided sources.  
Interpretation: optimizer hyperparameter tuning (especially betas/eps for AdamW) matters, particularly with batch-size changes; there is no direct evidence here favoring alternate optimizers in this short-run regime. This is an evidence gap regarding LAMB/Adafactor. Minimal discriminating experiment: within the 30‑minute budget, run 2–3 short variants changing only AdamW betas/eps used in the baseline logs; stop if validation BPB increases or training becomes unstable. Evidence vs conjecture: tuning betas is evidence‑supported as relevant [7]; choice of alternate optimizers is a gap.

## 5. Parameter allocation (matrices vs embeddings vs hashed n‑gram tables)
Evidence summary: no quantified comparisons of parameter allocation or of hashed n‑gram table overfitting vs benefit appear in the provided sources. The cramming work allows training from scratch and suggests sampling choices can help speedups but does not quantify cheap-memory module tradeoffs [1]. The hashed n‑gram memory in the baseline is not evaluated in the provided findings.  
Conclusion: evidence gap — require direct small‑run ablation on this exact baseline to assess BPB impact.

## 6. EMA, shared layers, progressive growth, positional encodings, multiscale context
Evidence summary: the provided sources do not report EMA effects, progressive growth, layer sharing, or RoPE variants for 30‑minute small runs. Curriculum and cramming describe data ordering and allowed architectures but do not provide these specific experiments [1], [5].  
Conclusion: evidence gaps for these mechanisms.

## 7. Throughput vs token budget — is more tokens always better?
Evidence summary: a report in the briefing notes that throughput gains allowing ~350M tokens sometimes worsened held‑out quality (user logs); the cramming and the “large-data vs repeated high‑quality data” analysis argue that more distinct tokens with few epochs tends to be better and that repeated use of same data loses utility [1], [3]. Rinas and microbatching papers show throughput can be raised substantially but emphasize distinguishing throughput improvements from effective training quality [4], [6]. Vyas et al. caution about assuming small‑batch noise benefits in single‑epoch regimes [7].  
Interpretation: faster configs that only increase repeated exposure to the same high‑utility subset may not improve—and can worsen—BPB in short runs; prioritize throughput that increases distinct token exposure (via better shuffling/loader) rather than repeated passes over the same small corpus. [1], [3], [4], [6], [7]

## Prioritized short list (top 6; rank by expected payoff per wall‑clock minute & clarity)
1. Fix/optimize data loader & global shuffle strategy (use Rinas‑style improvements or reservoir sampling) — evidence: throughput gains up to 89% and reservoir single‑pass guarantees [4], [2]. Test: baseline vs loader‑optimized run; pass if validation BPB improves controlling for tokens/sec.
2. Try simple curriculum vs random order (code‑LM short‑run evidence) — evidence: curriculum improved small code LMs trained <2 hours [5], [8]. Test: curriculum hybrid vs baseline; pass if lower validation BPB.
3. Microbatching to increase tokens/sec while logging per‑update effects — evidence: 4.8× throughput with 32 microbatches in one study [6]; but see batch‑size cautions [7]. Test: microbatch config that increases tokens/sec; pass only if BPB improves not just token count.
4. Compare baseline AdamW beta/eps variants (small sweep) — evidence: batch‑sensitivity of Adam betas reported [7]. Test: minimal beta tweaks; pass if BPB improves in same wall time.
5. Reservoir sampling single‑pass vs global shuffle for streamed data — evidence: algorithmic guarantees and recency properties [2]; Test: reservoir vs shuffle.
6. Avoid blindly preferring configurations that only increase token count via repeats — evidence: repeated use of high‑quality data loses utility [3]; Test: if faster config increases tokens but validation BPB worsens, revert.

## Evidence gaps (explicit)
- No primary results here quantify warmup/decay schedule shapes for 30‑minute/single‑accelerator LM training. [3], [7] do not provide concrete short‑run schedule numbers.  
- No primary comparisons of optimizer families (LAMB/Adafactor) in this regime are present. [7] only discusses Adam variants and tuning sensitivity.  
- No primary evaluation of EMA, hashed n‑gram table effectiveness, parameter allocation tradeoffs, progressive growth, or RoPE/relative positional variants for the strict short‑run small‑data regime appear in the provided sources. [1], [3], [5] lack these ablations.

## Minimal logging and reproducibility checklist (what to record)
- Wall‑clock start/end; tokens processed; tokens/sec and effective global‑batch and microbatch sizes; validation BPB and training loss at fixed wall‑time checkpoints; seed(s) used; data-ordering/loader method; exact optimizer betas/eps. (These items are prescribed so loader and tokens/sec confounders can be diagnosed; these logging items are consistent with the evidence that throughput and data ordering are major confounders.) [4], [6], [2], [3]

## Works Cited
[1] https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/geiping23a/geiping23a.pdf  
[2] https://aclanthology.org/P14-2112.pdf  
[3] https://arxiv.org/html/2506.21545v1  
[4] https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02368  
[5] https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-srw.44.pdf  
[6] https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3586074  
[7] https://arxiv.org/html/2507.07101v1  
[8] https://huggingface.co/papers/2407.10194

(Statements in the body are explicitly marked as evidence when directly supported by the cited items above; recommendations that go beyond those sources are presented as conjecture or experimental suggestions and are labelled as such in the relevant paragraphs.)
